app.title: Map Projektor
compare.description: Pick up to 5 countries and drag them across the map: each one stretches or shrinks as the projection does there.
compare.limitReached: 5 countries max. Remove one to add another.
compare.title: Compare
projection.aitoff.bestFor: Historical and reference use. Its equal-area descendant, Hammer, has mostly replaced it.
projection.aitoff.distorts: Both shape and area, moderately, worst near the outer edge of the ellipse.
projection.aitoff.name: Aitoff
projection.aitoff.preserves: Nothing exactly: a geometric compromise built for a pleasing outline.
projection.albers.bestFor: Mid-latitude regional maps of a single country or continent (its original purpose: the continental US).
projection.albers.distorts: Shape, more and more the further a region sits from those two parallels. Poor for global or equatorial use.
projection.albers.name: Albers
projection.albers.preserves: Area exactly, and shape stays accurate between its two standard parallels (here 20°N and 50°N).
projection.azimuthalEqualArea.bestFor: Maps centred on one region whose areas must stay comparable, such as a continent or a polar area.
projection.azimuthalEqualArea.distorts: Shape, more and more with distance from the centre. Regions near the antipode are squeezed into the outer rim.
projection.azimuthalEqualArea.name: Azimuthal Equal Area
projection.azimuthalEqualArea.preserves: Area exactly from its centre point outward, and direction from that same centre.
projection.eckert4.bestFor: Thematic climate and population maps: the same equal-area guarantee as Mollweide, with gentler shapes.
projection.eckert4.distorts: Shape at high latitudes, where landmasses compress toward the half-length pole lines.
projection.eckert4.name: Eckert IV
projection.eckert4.preserves: Area exactly, with a rounded outline that reads comfortably at world scale.
projection.equalEarth.bestFor: A modern replacement for Gall-Peters: true-size thematic maps that still look natural.
projection.equalEarth.distorts: Shape moderately near the poles, though far less severely than older equal-area projections.
projection.equalEarth.name: Equal Earth
projection.equalEarth.preserves: Area exactly, while keeping shapes visibly less stretched than Gall-Peters.
projection.equirectangular.bestFor: Simplicity and raw geographic data (it's just the coordinates), not display accuracy.
projection.equirectangular.distorts: Both shape and area, worsening toward the poles. A 1:1 lon/lat grid is not a neutral choice.
projection.equirectangular.name: Equirectangular
projection.equirectangular.preserves: Nothing exactly, but distances along meridians and the equator are true to scale.
projection.gallPeters.bestFor: Thematic maps where relative size matters more than recognisable shape (population, resources).
projection.gallPeters.distorts: Shape, severely: continents look stretched vertically near the equator and flattened near the poles.
projection.gallPeters.name: Gall-Peters
projection.gallPeters.preserves: Area exactly: every landmass is shown at its true relative size.
projection.hammer.bestFor: Whole-world equal-area maps, also used in astronomy for all-sky maps.
projection.hammer.distorts: Shape near the outer edge of the ellipse, though less severely than Aitoff or Mollweide.
projection.hammer.name: Hammer
projection.hammer.preserves: Area exactly, inheriting Aitoff's pleasing elliptical outline.
projection.mercator.bestFor: Nautical navigation and web maps at street-level zoom.
projection.mercator.distorts: Area, dramatically, away from the equator: Greenland looks as large as Africa despite being 14 times smaller.
projection.mercator.name: Mercator
projection.mercator.preserves: Angles and local shapes (conformal): a straight line on the map is a constant compass bearing.
projection.mollweide.bestFor: Global thematic maps (e.g. star charts, world distributions) where area is what matters.
projection.mollweide.distorts: Shape strongly near the outer edge of the ellipse, especially at high latitudes.
projection.mollweide.name: Mollweide
projection.mollweide.preserves: Area exactly, within an elliptical world outline.
projection.naturalEarth.bestFor: Wall maps and general reference where visual appeal matters more than any measurable property.
projection.naturalEarth.distorts: Area and shape both, mildly, worst at high latitudes near the rounded poles.
projection.naturalEarth.name: Natural Earth
projection.naturalEarth.preserves: Nothing exactly: a compromise tuned by eye to look natural at a glance.
projection.orthographic.bestFor: Intuitive 'globe' views and showing a single hemisphere or region in spatial context.
projection.orthographic.distorts: Area and shape increasingly toward the visible edge (the limb), where the surface is nearly edge-on.
projection.orthographic.name: Orthographic
projection.orthographic.preserves: The look of a globe seen from space. It is the only projection here that looks like a sphere.
projection.polarNorth.bestFor: Polar-region maps and anything where 'distance from this one point' is the property that matters.
projection.polarNorth.distorts: Area and shape severely near the outer edge, where Antarctica is stretched into a ring around the map.
projection.polarNorth.name: North Polar
projection.polarNorth.preserves: Distance from the North Pole to anywhere else. That is the one property equidistant guarantees.
projection.polarSouth.bestFor: Southern-hemisphere and Antarctic maps, a viewpoint almost never seen on a default world map.
projection.polarSouth.distorts: Area and shape severely near the outer edge, where the Arctic is stretched into the outer ring instead.
projection.polarSouth.name: South Polar
projection.polarSouth.preserves: Distance from the South Pole to anywhere else, same guarantee as the North Polar view mirrored.
projection.robinson.bestFor: General-purpose reference world maps where no single property needs to be exact.
projection.robinson.distorts: Everything a little (area, shape, distance) rather than any one thing a lot.
projection.robinson.name: Robinson
projection.robinson.preserves: Nothing exactly: a table-based compromise, tuned by eye rather than by a strict formula.
projection.sinusoidal.bestFor: Historical interest and equal-area maps where true distances along the parallels matter.
projection.sinusoidal.distorts: Shape, severely at the outer edges, with a strong diagonal shear at high latitudes and far from the central meridian.
projection.sinusoidal.name: Sinusoidal
projection.sinusoidal.preserves: Area exactly, and distance is true along every parallel and the central meridian.
projection.winkelTripel.bestFor: General-purpose world reference maps. National Geographic has used it since 1998.
projection.winkelTripel.distorts: A little of everything by design, the trade-off its name promises (a "tripel" compromise).
projection.winkelTripel.name: Winkel Tripel
projection.winkelTripel.preserves: Nothing exactly, but keeps area, angle, and distance distortion all simultaneously low.

tour.step.equalEarth.text: Same planet, drawn by Equal Earth: Greenland is back to its real size, 14 times smaller than Africa. Every button in this list redraws the world its own way.
tour.step.equalEarth.title: Now look at it again
tour.step.mercator.text: This is Mercator, the map of most classrooms and of online maps. Look at Greenland: it seems as large as Africa. Press Next and watch another projection redraw it.
tour.step.mercator.title: A map you know
tour.step.navigation.text: Zoom with these buttons or the mouse wheel, and drag to pan the map or spin the globe.
tour.step.navigation.title: Move around
tour.step.tools.text: Distortion grid, reference lines, light or dark theme, country size comparison and the facts about the current projection.
tour.step.tools.title: See the distortions
tour.step.views.text: Centre the map on another region, or turn it upside down. The view carries over when you switch projection.
tour.step.views.title: Change the point of view
view.africa.description: Centred near 20°E, the middle of the African continent. The natural framing for atlases of Africa, and a reminder that a Europe-centred map is a choice, not a fact of nature.
view.africa.name: Africa-centred
view.america.description: A common convention in American atlases, centred near 90°W: the Americas face you on the globe, and flat maps split the world through Asia.
view.america.name: America-centred
view.china.description: A common convention in Chinese school atlases, centred near 105°E: the world splits along the Atlantic instead of the Pacific.
view.china.name: China-centred
view.oceania.description: Centred near 150°E on the western Pacific: East Asia, Australia, New Zealand and the Pacific islands gathered around one ocean, as in atlases from Australia and East Asia.
view.oceania.name: Oceania-centred
view.southAmericaFlipped.description: South at the top, as on McArthur's Universal Corrective Map (1979) and the world map announced in 2025 by IBGE, Brazil's national mapping institute: a deliberate challenge to the idea that north has to be up.
view.southAmericaFlipped.name: South-up
view.world.description: Centred on the Greenwich meridian: the Atlantic-centred convention of most Western atlases, with Europe and West Africa in the middle.
view.world.name: Europe-centred
welcome.intro1: As we all know, the Earth is a sphere. (Sorry, flat earthers.)
welcome.intro2: Squashing it onto a flat map is where it gets awkward: shapes, areas, distances and directions can't all survive the trip, so every projection picks what to keep and what to bend. Each choice has its perks and its little lies. On a Mercator map, Greenland looks as big as Africa, which is about 14 times larger.
welcome.intro3: This tool lets you see those trade-offs for yourself.
welcome.title: Welcome to Map Projektor!
